items.title: PHP2Shell enters KEV as Palo Alto reports attacks on internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces — and Siemens lists its RUGGEDCOM APE1808 firewall module as affected
items.content_text: CISA added the two PHP flaws known as PHP2Shell, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS v4.0 9.2, PHP Group), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 October with a 29 October federal deadline. Amazon says attempts began on 17 October, four days before PHP shipped fixes, and researchers at Perplexity (Adel Karimi), with Expel’s Marcus Hutchins concurring, confirmed working remote code execution against a honeypot over 24–25 October. No victim organisation has been named, CISA did not describe the activity, and Sophos and Unit 42 have withdrawn earlier reports of successful compromises. The boundary angle is what is new this week. Palo Alto Networks’ advisory on the PHP flaws, raised to Critical and updated on 27–28 October, reports active exploitation targeting PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet — the web interface and XML API on PA-Series, VM-Series and Panorama; GlobalProtect is not affected. Palo Alto scores it CVSS v4.0 9.2, or 5.2 where management access is restricted to a jump box, and its hotfixes are rolling out between 21 and 30 October, with some branches still pending; they also cover the Brotli decoder flaw CVE-2026-111497, which CISA added to KEV on 27 October. Siemens’ advisory SSA-566512 (23 October) lists RUGGEDCOM APE1808, an application module for Siemens’ ruggedised RUGGEDCOM platform that can host a Palo Alto firewall, as affected when it runs PAN-OS 10.2 to 12.2, with remediation through Siemens customer support plus Palo Alto’s workarounds. PHP itself is fixed in 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, and CISA has published a SIGMA detection rule. Palo Alto names no victims, and no rail or transit victim has been reported. It leads because it is exploited, unauthenticated code execution on a firewall class that guards many railway IT/OT boundaries, with a ruggedised Siemens variant built for the kind of trackside, communications and traction-power networks where RUGGEDCOM hardware is common (editorial assessment).

items.title: Renfe passenger data was taken through compromised Adif servers; Adif says no rail-operations system was touched
items.content_text: Adif, Spain’s state railway infrastructure manager, detected unusual activity late on 24 September, took its websites offline as a precaution and restored them on 26 September. On 25 September the train operator Renfe said passenger data, mainly names and email addresses, had been obtained from Adif servers compromised earlier; it reported no impact on banking or financial data and has given no passenger count. Adif says no system related to railway operations was affected and trains ran normally. A 500 GB haul and AI-assisted tooling, aired in Spanish media and in Shieldworkz’s 30 September analysis, remain unconfirmed by either company, and no actor has been named. Spain’s Ministry of Transport later said the data taken was limited, most likely names and email addresses with no bank, payment or identity data, that the intrusion followed several weeks of attack attempts that had been detected and blocked, and that rail service was not interrupted. This is an IT and customer-data incident, not an OT one. It stays on this page as the most recent confirmed intrusion at a national rail operator we have found, and because it came through a partner link both sides trusted by design; we found no newer statement from either company as of 28 October.

items.title: CISA, the FBI and partners say SafePay ransomware has hit at least 600 organizations since August 2024 — through stolen credentials, VPN logins and old firewall flaws
items.content_text: The FBI and CISA, with the US Secret Service, Germany’s LKA Rheinland-Pfalz, the UK’s National Crime Agency and the North West Regional Organised Crime Unit, published joint advisory AA26-293A on 20 October. It says SafePay, a closed group that does not use affiliates, has affected at least 600 organizations from multiple critical-infrastructure sectors since August 2024, in North and South America, Europe and Australia, and it gives indicators and techniques observed from November 2024 to August 2026. Entry is through exposed or brute-forced credentials, VPN access — the advisory cites Mullvad VPN addresses — phished accounts and automated exploitation of edge-device flaws; Cybersecurity Dive names CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2023-20269, which the CVE records place in Cisco ASA and Firepower Threat Defense software and which CISA lists in KEV with known ransomware use. Once inside, the group steals data before encrypting and hinders recovery by deleting shadow copies and resetting network-attached storage that holds backups. The coverage we read names no transport victim. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: ransomware outages at rail operators typically begin in IT, and remote-access VPNs and NAS-based backups sit in the corporate networks that dispatch, maintenance and passenger-information systems depend on.

items.title: The FBI and Secret Service say FortiBleed credential theft against FortiGate firewalls is still running — across every critical-infrastructure sector, with no CVE to patch
items.content_text: The FBI and the US Secret Service issued a joint advisory on Tuesday 6 October warning that the FortiBleed campaign against internet-facing Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways remains an active threat. It is not a software vulnerability and has no CVE: per the agencies, it exploits reused or leaked credentials and legacy SHA-256 password storage. Researchers describe credential stuffing and spraying from leak dumps and infostealer logs, offline cracking of extracted password hashes on a GPU cluster, and a Go-based sniffer that passively captures authentication traffic across 24 protocols. Some owners were locked out after the attackers created their own administrator accounts and deleted or reset the legitimate ones. The agencies say compromised firewalls have served as ransomware entry points, and the FBI advisory links the access to Payload ransomware. Cybersecurity Dive reports that targets span all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors — a list that by definition includes transportation systems — naming energy, communications, and food and agriculture among them. The most-cited scale figure, more than 86,644 working device credentials across 194 countries, is SOCRadar’s count as of 19 June, not a new tally; SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments stemming from the access and describes the operator as a Russian-speaking access broker, which is a researcher assessment, not agency attribution. No OT system compromise and no rail victim has been described. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: FortiGate is one of the most common firewalls at the IT/OT boundary of railroads and transit agencies, and a stolen administrator credential there is a way to rewrite segmentation without exploiting anything.

items.title: Attackers took over web-managed refrigeration controllers at about 700 French supermarkets — a food-sector attack, and a direct lesson for contractor-managed station and depot plant
items.content_text: From the night of 11–12 October, attackers remotely took control of internet-reachable refrigeration management controllers in French supermarkets and forced them into continuous or extended defrost, with setpoints of up to about 50 °C, spoiling stock; the Paris prosecutor reports outbreaks of fire at some sites. A second wave on the night of 12–13 October hit stores with Dixell controllers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on 13 October that about 700 of France’s roughly 10,000 supermarkets were affected, and Carrefour, Coopérative U, E.Leclerc, Intermarché/Netto and Monoprix have confirmed impact. CERT-FR’s alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 named Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers on 12 October, added Copeland and Dixell xweb on 13 October, and in its 16 October update says attack campaigns are probably still ongoing. As of 28 October CERT-FR’s alert was still at version 3 of 16 October, and no new attack nights had been reported since 13 October. Danfoss and Copeland say most affected units are older, end-of-life models. No group has claimed the attack, no ransom has been demanded and the entry route has not been established; the national cyber agency ANSSI has mobilised, and the Paris prosecutor’s cybercrime section has opened an inquiry. Reports of targeting in other European countries come from one security firm, Sekoia, and have not been confirmed by any foreign authority. Separately, Claroty’s Team82 showed on 13 October that an AI coding agent, steered by a researcher, reproduced a previously disclosed Danfoss exploit chain to root in about 28 minutes; it does not say those flaws were used in France. This is not a rail incident and it does not count toward this page’s threat level. It is here as our editorial lesson: stations, depots and tunnels run the same kind of contractor-supported, web-managed plant — HVAC, ventilation, pumping, lighting — and this attack needed little more than reachability and outdated controllers.

items.title: ESET documents a Belarus-aligned group’s first destructive attack in Europe — on a Ukrainian manufacturer with an important role in the country’s transportation sector
items.content_text: ESET’s APT Activity Report covering April to September 2026, published on 28 October, says that according to its telemetry the Belarus-aligned group it tracks as FrostyNeighbor attacked a manufacturing company in Ukraine that plays an important role in the country’s transportation sector, and calls it the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned actor that ESET has documented in the European theatre. ESET does not name the company, the malware or the date, and describes no effect on transport operations. The same report notes the Iran-aligned OilRig subgroup FilthyFeline taking over activity against a cellular data provider in Uzbekistan, and North Korea’s DeceptiveDevelopment moving from fake job interviews to compromising source-code repositories with stolen developer credentials. Six days earlier, on 22 October, ESET described how the Russia-aligned UAC-0099 gained access to a Ukrainian grain firm through a spearphishing attachment in July 2025, after which Sandworm wiped data there in September 2025 by pushing a deletion tool through Active Directory Group Policy; ESET assesses that UAC-0099 can act as an initial-access group for Sandworm. All attributions are ESET’s assessments. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: transport manufacturers and freight logistics are now inside the destructive-attack target set in this conflict, and a wipe pushed through Group Policy reaches every domain-joined machine, including those that support operations.

items.title: US authorities seize the scanning and phishing tools of a China-based contractor whose named targets included airports in Japan and Poland and a US power company
items.content_text: The Justice Department and FBI announced on 8 October court-authorised seizures, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, of domains behind two tools: Microscan, a Python web application carrying more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts, and FishHub, a spear-phishing and malware-delivery service. US authorities tie both to Integrity Technology Group, a China-based company sanctioned last year. CyberScoop describes the tools as Flax Typhoon-linked, while Cybersecurity Dive says the activity mimics that group and others such as Ethereal Panda rather than equating them. A Mirai-variant IoT botnet supported Microscan, and a joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory notes persistence through VPN software. Court documents name Microscan targets including a South Carolina power company, airports in Japan and Poland, gas and power companies in Taiwan and a multinational NGO, with Taiwanese universities hit by FishHub phishing; no target’s compromise is confirmed. CISA’s Chris Butera said Chinese government-affiliated actors continue to position themselves within critical-infrastructure networks, including operational technology systems. No rail operator is named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: transportation hubs are on the target list, and pre-positioning of this kind typically starts with exactly what Microscan automated — scanning internet-facing services for known flaws.

items.title: Mandiant says ShinyHunters is back exploiting Oracle PeopleSoft by encoding one letter past WAF rules — transportation is among the sectors with compromised systems
items.content_text: Google Threat Intelligence and Mandiant reported on 25 September a renewed mass-exploitation campaign by UNC6240, the group known as ShinyHunters, against CVE-2026-35273, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (the /PSEMHUB/ path), rated CVSS v3.1 9.8. The flaw was first exploited as a zero-day against academic institutions in late May and early June, and Oracle has had a fix out since June. The new wave requests /%50SEMHUB/ instead: WAF rules that match the literal path miss it, and WebLogic decodes and routes the request anyway, reaching, in Mandiant’s words, “systems whose operators may have believed their WAF rules had mitigated the exposure”. Mandiant counts “dozens of systems” compromised globally across higher education, technology and IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government, names no victims, and says it has notified more than 100 organisations whose addresses matched vulnerable endpoints. The tooling includes JSP web shells, Neo-reGeorg tunnels, a SIDEEYE backdoor delivered in a trojanised Light Alloy media-player installer, and MeshAgent. CISA has listed CVE-2026-35273 in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue since 12 June 2026 and marks it as known to be used in ransomware campaigns. Since then the FBI has said, on 6 October, that a breach of its own jobs portal resulted from a contractor that failed to apply a patch explicitly issued for the platform — which Reuters, citing unnamed sources, identified as Oracle PeopleSoft — and on 9 October it announced another arrest of a suspected ShinyHunters member, saying the group has breached more than 140 organisations. Oracle’s October 2026 quarterly Critical Patch Update has since been released. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: many transit authorities and railroads run PeopleSoft for HR, payroll and finance, and a web shell on that tier puts employee records and whatever directory and database credentials the application holds within an attacker’s reach. It is an IT-side risk, not an OT one.

items.title: Nozomi’s summer OT telemetry ranks transportation second for alerts per customer, behind manufacturing
items.content_text: Nozomi Networks Labs published its June–August 2026 OT and IoT telemetry review on 12 October. Ranked by alerts per organisation, manufacturing came first, transportation second and energy, utilities and waste third, displacing government. Credential-related techniques made up roughly a third of detections. Among alerts Nozomi could attribute to an actor, Scattered Spider accounted for close to half, and Russia-linked or Russian-speaking actors together for more than a third. Siemens PLCs and Rockwell products were among the most-detected vulnerable products, and Nozomi says 58 percent of 2026 vulnerabilities rate High or Critical, up from 48 percent in 2025. Two cautions apply: alerts per organisation measures what Nozomi customers’ sensors flagged, not a count of attacks, and the actor names are telemetry attributions, not confirmed intrusions. The report does not break out rail. The reading for rail is our editorial assessment: transportation’s place in the ranking reflects a sector whose networks are increasingly instrumented and noisy, and the credential share supports putting identity controls ahead of exotic OT exploits.

items.title: Dragos sees old worms — Sality, Conficker, WannaCry — turning up more often in OT incident calls, and warns the wrong cleanup can hurt more than the infection
items.content_text: Dragos’s Lesley Carhart and Jan Hoff wrote on 15 October that requests for help with legacy commodity malware such as Sality, Gammima, WannaCry and Conficker have risen sharply in recent years, and that many OT networks Dragos is called into carry between 20 and 70 distinct commodity-malware variants across several subnets, often on systems older than Windows XP Service Pack 2. They attribute the rise to more networking and remote access, better visibility, and regulation that expects critical-infrastructure networks to be clean. Their answer is a “Now / Next / Never” framework, with a white paper, for deciding what to clean immediately, what to schedule and what to leave contained, and a warning that the wrong cleanup can be riskier than the infection itself. No actor or campaign is involved. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: signalling-support, SCADA and passenger-information estates are full of long-lived Windows hosts that suppliers certify and operators cannot simply rebuild, which is exactly the population Dragos describes.

items.title: FDD warns that NATO reinforcement across Europe runs through civilian ports and railways with uneven cyber rules — and that Chinese-linked firms operate terminals in about half the EU ports NATO relies on
items.content_text: The Foundation for Defense of Democracies published a report on 28 September by Jiwon Ma, a senior policy analyst at its Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation, titled Strengthening NATO Through Military Mobility and Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity. As reported by Industrial Cyber, it finds that three port groups — COSCO Shipping, China Merchants Group and Hutchison Port Holdings — own or operate terminals in roughly half of the EU ports considered critical to NATO operations; that firms FDD describes as Chinese state-linked hold stakes in more than 30 European port terminals, including facilities designated to receive US forces; and that they operate at no fewer than 14 of the 29 European ports near NATO naval facilities. For rail, the report’s point is scale and dependency: it notes that moving a single light division can take up to 200 trains, and that rail, unlike military air transport, has no mechanism for pooling assets, so it recommends jointly procuring or designating a minimum pool of dual-use heavy-lift wagons. Its cyber finding is that governance split across NATO, the EU and national authorities leaves the civilian transport operators that alliance forces depend on without consistent security standards. Other recommendations include aligning investment with reinforcement plans, annual national military-mobility annexes, organising NATO cyber-defence work around critical-infrastructure operators, tighter EU investment screening on military corridors, measures against satellite interference, and treating cyber workforce shortages as a defence priority. This is policy analysis from a think tank, not an incident or a government finding, and it names no compromised operator. The rail relevance for European infrastructure managers and freight operators on reinforcement corridors is our editorial assessment: a defence role can arrive without a matching security requirement, and the terminal at the port end of a rail movement may be run by a party whose systems you exchange data with but do not control.

items.title: Two August counts, one direction: Comparitech logged a record 997 ransomware attacks and NCC Group 1,073, with industrial victims the largest share — and a newer group, Aurora, lists transportation among its targets
items.content_text: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — about 32 a day, 23 percent more than July’s 809 and above the previous monthly record of 988 — with utility, healthcare and business-services attacks singled out as the categories behind the rise. NCC Group’s August review, reported by Industrial Cyber on 28 September, counts 1,073 attacks, up 12 percent from 960 in July, with the industrial sector the largest target at 329 attacks (31 percent), North America at 473 (44 percent) and Europe at 276 (26 percent); Qilin led with 164, overtaking The Gentlemen. NCC also profiles Aurora, a ransomware-as-a-service group active since late April 2026 whose targets include manufacturing, legal, research and development, and transportation: it gets in through VPN exploitation and credential harvesting, then encrypts hypervisors, taking every hosted virtual machine down at once. Both counts rest on leak-site claims and disclosure practice, which is why the totals differ; claimed victims are not confirmed victims, and neither tracker names a rail operator. For rail and transit the exposure is rarely the signalling system itself — it is dispatch support, crew management, maintenance planning, fare collection and passenger information, much of which now runs as virtual machines on a small number of hypervisors.

items.title: DOE and Idaho National Laboratory start a weekly Cyber-Informed Engineering series — rail’s fail-safe tradition is the same idea, applied on purpose
items.content_text: The Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER) and Idaho National Laboratory announced on 13 October a weekly “CIE Back-to-School” series that works through the twelve principles of Cyber-Informed Engineering one at a time, each with an overview, a case study and questions for engineers, starting with consequence-focused design. A new, simplified CIE Handbook is due at the end of the series. The argument behind CIE is that the security question belongs upstream, in design: identify the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineer them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system staying trustworthy. The series is aimed at energy infrastructure and is voluntary guidance, not regulation. The rail connection is our editorial assessment. Interlocking, fail-safe signalling and vital logic exist precisely so that an upstream failure cannot produce an unsafe movement; CIE asks that those principles be applied deliberately to newer digital systems rather than assumed to still hold. It is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure.

items.title: Google’s threat intelligence group documents a credential campaign run end to end by autonomous agents in under six hours — and exploited vulnerabilities now arriving at about 18 a month
items.content_text: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated group completed a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours using an autonomous multi-agent framework, with the agents rather than human operators carrying it through. GTIG separately observed actors stealing AI API credentials and running unauthorised workloads inside victims’ own cloud tenants across healthcare, government and media, and its guidance is to assume every actor is now using AI to some degree. On 30 September GTIG followed with data on vulnerability discovery and exploitation: monthly disclosures roughly doubled from 5,045 in January 2026 to 10,477 in July and reached 10,740 in August, while exploited vulnerabilities averaged 18 a month from January to August against 10.5 a month in 2025 — 141 distinct exploited flaws in eight months, against 127 in all of 2025. Edge and security appliances made up 14 percent of the exploited flaws, and more than 65 percent of those carried GTIG’s high or critical risk ratings; half of AI-discovered vulnerabilities were remote code execution, against 26 percent across the wider CVE ecosystem. GTIG does not discuss OT, industrial control systems or rail; that connection is ours. The rail consequence is arithmetic, not novelty. Credential phishing against dispatchers, crew callers, maintenance planners and contractor accounts is the standard opening move, and a campaign that completes inside six hours finishes well before a Monday-morning review — and comfortably inside the overnight window when the operations control centre is staffed but the security team is not. More exploited edge flaws each month also means the remote-access gear on this page’s advisory list will keep arriving faster than a slow patch cycle can absorb.

items.title: Arista patches a third exploited VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day in four months, and CISA adds it to KEV — the console that configures the SD-WAN edge at every connected site
items.content_text: Arista disclosed on 22 October that CVE-2026-114625, an SQL injection flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator, was detected by Arista and is known to be actively exploited. Any authenticated user, down to the lowest built-in tenant role, can use it to gain operator privileges and act as a local “superuser operator”. Arista, as CVE numbering authority, rates it CVSS v3.1 9.9 and v4.0 9.4. Fixed releases are 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12; Arista-hosted and dedicated orchestrators are already patched, and VeloCloud gateways and edges are not affected. SecurityWeek lists two IP addresses seen in the attacks and quotes Arista: “There is no configuration that can prevent the exposure,” so updating is the remedy. It is the third exploited orchestrator zero-day in four months, after CVE-2026-16812 in July and CVE-2026-93952 in September, and CISA added it to KEV late on 23 October with a 26 October federal deadline, which has passed; this page’s previous edition wrongly showed it as not listed. No victims, sectors or actor have been named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: where stations, depots and wayside sites hang off an SD-WAN, the orchestrator holds the configuration of every edge, so whoever controls it can reroute traffic or open paths into the networks behind them.

items.title: Siemens confirms its signed Software Center program is being abused to plant malware on Windows PCs, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
items.content_text: Siemens said on 19 October that CVE-2026-110936, a DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens Software Center — the program that downloads, installs, activates and updates Siemens software customers have bought — is being exploited. Attackers bundle a genuine, validly signed copy of version 3.5.8.7 with their own DLLs in an installer pushed through ClickFix lures, so the trusted program runs the attackers’ code; Siemens tells customers to look for it even on PCs where Software Center was never installed. Siemens links the activity to the “Romulus” ClickFix campaign, names no malware family, and says no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached to its knowledge. Version 4.0.9.8 fixes the flaw. CISA added it to KEV on 20 October, due 3 November, and republished the advisory on 22 October with Transportation Systems among the listed sectors. As of 28 October Siemens’ advisory was still at version 1.2 and we found no newer campaign reporting. No rail victim has been reported. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: engineering workstations that trust anything Siemens-signed are exactly what this abuses, and the federal deadline is now less than a week away.

items.title: PHP2Shell in industrial software: Schneider now has a fix for EcoStruxure Control Engineering, ABB plans APROL patches, and Siemens and Rockwell are still checking
items.content_text: Industrial vendors have spent the week working out which of their products embed the PHP flaws CISA listed in KEV on 26 October (the boundary-firewall side is this edition’s top story). Schneider Electric’s notice SESB-2026-295-01 reached version 2.0.0 on 26 October and now says remediation is available for EcoStruxure Control Engineering, which version 1.0.0 had listed without a fix: the update applies automatically where the virtual machine can reach the debian.org and sury.org repositories, and otherwise customers request a patch from Schneider support. EcoStruxure Security Expert is fixed in 1.48.4.0, and LINEoptimize (formerly ProLeiT Plant iT LMS) is remediated through ProLeiT support. ABB’s B&R advisory SA26P015 (23 October) lists the APROL process-control system up to R 4.4-65 as affected, with patches planned for 26 and 29 October, and ABB advisory 4HZK000017 tells users of ABB MES installations that include DokuWiki to update PHP or shut DokuWiki down; ABB scores both CVSS v3.1 9.8. Siemens has published SSA-566435, listing 31 software products as not affected, and SSA-166980, listing 20 Smart Infrastructure products — among them Desigo CC, Siveillance and SiPass — as not affected, and says its evaluation continues. Rockwell’s SD1802 (23 October) confirms no affected products while its review continues, and Moxa has published a response notice, MPSA-260001, whose content we could not verify. No compromise of an OT product has been reported. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: PHP runs unseen inside the web interfaces of engineering, building-management and access-control tools found in stations, depots and control centres, and vendor notices are the only reliable way to learn which embedded copies need fixing.

items.title: Moxa fixes a man-in-the-middle flaw in its Remote Connect client — but its OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway is end-of-life, with static keys and an SMS command-injection flaw that will not be fixed
items.content_text: Moxa published advisory MPSA-269510 on 27 October for three flaws. CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6, Moxa) affects the MRC Client of Moxa Remote Connect Suite, versions 1.0.0 to 4.2.0: because the client does not properly validate certificates when it takes an OpenVPN configuration supplied by the server, an attacker positioned between client and server could impersonate the server and read or alter the connection. Version 4.2.2 is not affected and, according to CERT-FR, the fix is obtained through Moxa technical support. The other two affect the OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway: CVE-2026-111460 (v4.0 7.7), private keys for HTTPS and the device certificate authority embedded statically in the firmware, and CVE-2026-111461 (v4.0 7.5), an operating-system command injection that an attacker with the required privileges can reach when SMS management is enabled. The gateway is end-of-life and no fix will be issued; Moxa’s mitigations are to reset the device so it regenerates its keys and to keep SMS management disabled, which is the default. No exploitation has been reported, and none of the three is in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: Moxa networking and cellular equipment is common across railways — on rolling stock, at stations and in wayside and telemetry cabinets — and remote-access clients like MRC are how engineers reach those sites from outside.

items.title: Fortinet has shipped fixes for critical and high-severity flaws in FortiOS, FortiManager and three other products, WaterISAC says — with CVE details held back until 10 November
items.content_text: WaterISAC reported in a TLP:CLEAR notification on 27 October that Fortinet has released a coordinated set of updates for critical and high-severity vulnerabilities in FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, found through Fortinet’s AI-assisted security testing. CVE identifiers, scores and technical details are due with public advisories on Fortinet’s PSIRT page on 10 November; until then, scanners that work from CVEs will not flag affected devices, so WaterISAC advises checking firmware versions directly. The fixed releases it lists are FortiOS 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 and 7.2.14; FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12 and 7.2.13; FortiMail 8.0.2, 7.6.7 and 7.4.9; and FortiAuthenticator 8.0.4 and 6.6.11. WaterISAC says no active exploitation has been reported. This rests on a single source — we found no matching Fortinet publication — so no CVE or score is given here. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: FortiGate is among the most common firewalls at railway IT/OT boundaries, FortiManager is how many managed providers run them (see the Peerstitch card), and the gap between fixes and disclosure is time in which attackers can compare old and new builds.

items.title: The FortiOS flaw behind Unit 42’s Peerstitch case is in KEV — attackers reached it through a provider’s FortiManager and exposed more than 500 managed firewalls
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2025-61624, a path-traversal flaw in the FortiOS command-line interface that also affects FortiProxy, FortiPAM and FortiSwitchManager, to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October federal deadline. Fortinet rates it Medium because the attacker needs privileged, authenticated access; it fixed the flaw in April 2026 and now marks it known exploited. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 reported on 14 October how it was used: at a telecommunications managed service provider, attackers exploited FortiManager CVE-2024-47575 and took configurations, serial numbers and credential material for more than 500 managed FortiGates, then used CVE-2025-61624 to gain root on managed firewalls and drop a loader Unit 42 calls PEERSTITCH with an SSH reverse-shell back door. Unit 42 describes the 500-plus as exposure of configuration and credential material, not confirmed intrusion into the provider’s customers. It tracks the cluster as CL-STA-0954 (UNC5820), notes overlaps with suspected nation-state intrusions and names no state. The CVE record also lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808, an industrial appliance that runs Fortinet’s firewall software. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: station and depot firewalls are often run by a managed provider through FortiManager, which makes the provider’s management plane part of your boundary.

items.title: Ivanti Connect Secure: a three-bug chain gave attackers root on fully patched VPNs — one CVE is fixed and in KEV, the privilege-escalation link is not
items.content_text: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that CVE-2026-104935 in Connect Secure had been exploited against a limited number of customers. The CVE covers two flaws — an authentication bypass by spoofing and a file write — that together let a remote, unauthenticated attacker run commands; Ivanti rates it CVSS v3.1 8.6. Volexity, which found the activity during an incident response, says the attackers added a third bug, a privilege escalation that has no CVE and no patch yet, to reach root on an appliance that was fully patched at the time. Exploitation dates from at least early October: Volexity’s case begins on 3 October and Defused saw activity from 1 October. Volexity tracks the operator as UTA0576, a new actor. It left no web shell or backdoor and ran commands through the exploit requests themselves, then stole LDAP and domain credentials, queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, Kerberoasted, sprayed passwords, sniffed LDAP traffic and wiped the appliance’s logs. Volexity has only low confidence that the motive is criminal rather than espionage. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 13 October with a 16 October deadline and, like Volexity, warns that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect this compromise, because the chain patches code in memory and restores configuration. Fixed releases are 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1; Ivanti said a fix for the third bug would follow in the coming weeks; as of 28 October we had found no Ivanti fix for it. No rail or transit victim has been named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: Connect Secure is a common VPN for contractors and remote engineers, and this actor went straight for the directory credentials that unlock what sits behind it.

items.title: NetScaler: a fourth critical SAML flaw lands on top of three exploited zero-days — builds that fixed September’s bugs need upgrading again, and patching does not evict an intruder
items.content_text: Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-107406 in bulletin CTX697191 on the evening of 8 October, and it was widely reported on 9 October: a memory overflow in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider, which Citrix says may lead to remote code execution or denial of service. It is rated CVSS v4.0 9.5, there is no workaround, Citrix says it is not aware of exploitation, and it was not in KEV as of CISA’s 27 October catalogue. The catch is the builds many operators installed in the past three weeks: as reported from Citrix’s bulletin, 14.1-73.37 to 14.1-73.41 and 13.1-64.23 to 13.1-64.28 remain vulnerable when the appliance acts as a SAML identity provider, so those must be upgraded again, to 14.1-73.46 or 13.1-64.29 or later (FIPS and NDcPP builds are listed separately). In guidance reported on 12 October, CISA urged customers to patch, warned that attackers use the crash bug CVE-2026-88779 to force reboots so that code planted through CVE-2026-88771 runs, and released detection rules. That sits on top of the exploited trio already in KEV: CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, each CVSS v4 9.5 and listed on 27 September, and CVE-2026-88779, listed on 4 October, which Citrix and watchTowr describe as denial of service. Mandiant ties the campaign to suspected state-nexus actors, names no group and counts dozens of affected organisations in North America and Europe; Arctic Wolf’s figure of at least 78 counts targeted organisations, not confirmed victims; Shadowserver sees more than 20,000 exposed or potentially vulnerable appliances. Reported post-exploitation tooling includes custom PHP web shells, and Mandiant warns that upgrading alone does not remove access an intruder already has. No rail or transit victim has been named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for supplier and remote-engineer access, and on many railways and transit agencies it is the path by which signalling, SCADA and fare-system contractors reach the OT DMZ.

items.title: A suspected PRC-nexus actor exploited a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day from late August — now in KEV, and the kind of console suppliers use to reach plant PCs
items.content_text: BeyondTrust and Google Threat Intelligence Group disclosed on 15 October that CVE-2026-102764, a flaw in Remote Support’s internal messaging components that lets attackers perform file operations on the appliance, had been exploited as a zero-day since late August. BeyondTrust, as CVE numbering authority, scores it CVSS v4.0 9.3, and every Remote Support release up to 26.2.3 is affected. GTIG attributes the exploitation, and the follow-on SAWFLY web shell and BARECLAW tunneller, to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor it tracks as ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221), on the basis of tooling and tradecraft overlap. SecurityWeek reports two appliances compromised, one hosted by BeyondTrust and one self-hosted; the attackers gained root, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the tool’s file transfer to pull documents from users’ desktops. BeyondTrust shipped a fix, patch BT26-05-RS, on 8 October and had patched its SaaS customers by 9 October; self-hosted appliances without automatic updates must be patched by hand, and releases older than 24.3.1 must be upgraded first. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 16 October with a federal deadline of 19 October, which has passed. GTIG names no victims or sectors. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: remote-support consoles of this kind are how many signalling, SCADA and building-systems suppliers reach the engineering workstations they commissioned, and a console under someone else’s control reaches everything its sessions do.

items.title: Six more exploited flaws enter KEV in three days — PAN-OS management, Cisco’s email gateway, a Windows Mark-of-the-Web bypass, AhsayCBS backup and Atlassian Data Center
items.content_text: Beyond Ivanti, CISA added six exploited flaws to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 13, 14 and 15 October, each with a three-day federal deadline. CVE-2026-96951, listed on 13 October, is the exploited zero-day in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday: a Windows Shell security-feature bypass that evades Mark of the Web, so downloaded files run without the usual warning; it needs user interaction and is scored CVSS v3.1 8.8. The release as a whole fixed more than 1,400 CVEs. CVE-2026-0322, listed on 14 October, lets an authenticated attacker with network access to the PAN-OS management interface run code as root on PA-Series, VM-Series and Panorama (CVSS v4.0 8.6 per Palo Alto); Palo Alto reports very limited exploitation and published attacker IP addresses. CVE-2026-76519, also 14 October and scored CVSS 9.8 by Cisco, lets an unauthenticated sender write files and run commands as root on Cisco Secure Email Gateway through a crafted attachment, where file reputation is enabled on a mail policy and Content Scanner Tools are older than 25.3.0.5525; it is the second exploited flaw in that product in a month. AhsayCBS CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134, listed the same day, chain an authentication flaw and a command injection in a backup server; Huntress saw them used to plant web shells and cryptocurrency miners, and Ahsay says its August patches were incomplete. CVE-2026-21589, listed on 15 October, lets an unauthenticated attacker read known files from the web root of Atlassian Data Center products including Confluence, Jira and Bitbucket. On 8 October CISA had also listed five much older flaws, in ISC BIND, Apache Struts, Strapi, ONLYOFFICE Docs and ProFTPD. No rail victim is named in any of these. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: PAN-OS often sits at the IT/OT boundary, Windows engineering workstations and HMIs are where a Mark-of-the-Web bypass lands, and the backup server is what a ransomware crew wants to own before it encrypts.

items.title: SonicWall SMA1000: a CVSS 10 pre-authentication flaw drew exploitation attempts within two days of the fix — not in KEV, and not a confirmed breach
items.content_text: SonicWall published advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 on 6–7 October for CVE-2026-102255, a server-side request forgery in the WorkPlace interface of SMA1000 secure-access appliances (SMA 6210, 7210 and 8200v). Reached through an unintended alternate path, it lets an unauthenticated attacker make the appliance send requests to its own internal functions; CISA’s enrichment scores it CVSS v3.1 10.0, and SonicWall calls it maximum severity. The same release fixed three authenticated flaws: CVE-2026-102256, an administrator command injection; CVE-2026-102257, a Zip Slip in the management console; and CVE-2026-102258, a stored cross-site scripting bug. Defused saw its first hits on SMA1000 decoys on 8 October, and Previdian counted 135 attempts from two US addresses. Those are attempts against sensors: no source has established a successful breach of a customer network, and the CVE was not in KEV as of CISA’s 27 October catalogue; some threat feeds now mark it as exploited, but no source has confirmed that. Fixed builds are 12.4.3-03670 and 12.5.0-03082 or later; there is no workaround, and SMA 100 and firewall SSL VPN are not affected. SMA1000 has been exploited repeatedly in 2026, so attempts this fast are not a surprise. No rail victim is named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: SMA1000 is a secure-access gateway of the kind suppliers and remote staff use to reach operational support systems.

items.title: CISA’s 22–27 October ICS releases are light for rail: ICONICS SCADA products with three legacy lines that will never be fixed, plus EPICS Base and a video encoder
items.content_text: Beyond its republication of Siemens’ October advisories, covered in the Siemens card below, the CISA ICS advisories we could confirm for the window are three. ICSA-26-300-02 (27 October) republishes Mitsubishi Electric’s ICONICS advisory 2026-006 of 15 October: CVE-2026-16438, an incorrect privilege assignment rated CVSS v3.1 9.1, two weak password-recovery flaws (CVE-2026-16436 at 8.1 and CVE-2026-16437 at 6.4) and the libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 (8.2), across GENESIS, GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI, IoTWorX, MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz. GENESIS 11.04 and release 10.98 of the GENESIS64 family fix them, but no fix is planned for MC Works64, GENESIS32 or BizViz, which Mitsubishi Electric says should be replaced; meanwhile it advises replacing the password-recovery challenge file with a blank one and restricting write access to it. ICSA-26-300-01 (27 October) covers four network-reachable flaws in EPICS Base 7.0.10 and earlier, the open-source control toolkit used at accelerators and research facilities, including an integer overflow rated CVSS v3.1 9.8 / v4.0 9.3 (CVE-2026-114595); 7.0.11 fixes them. ICSA-26-295-01 (22 October) covers nine flaws in the Kiloview E3 video encoder, fixed in firmware 1.30. CISA lists Critical Manufacturing, not transportation, for the two 27 October advisories and reports no known exploitation for any of the three. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: ICONICS software turns up as the HMI and energy-monitoring layer in facilities, including stations, depots and control buildings, and unfixable legacy lines are exactly what lingers in long-lived installations.

items.title: CISA’s 20 October ICS batch: a WAGO controller flaw that turns a low-privileged login into root, and Windows CAN-bus drivers that can be crashed — both labelled for transportation
items.content_text: CISA published five ICS advisories on 20 October, and two list Transportation Systems among the sectors using the affected products. ICSA-26-293-02 republishes WAGO’s CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-096 for controllers on WAGO’s Linux-based firmware below 4.10.0 (FW32): CC100, PFC100 G2, PFC200 G2, TP600, Edge Controller and WP400. CVE-2026-80466 lets a low-privileged remote user inject operating-system commands through routing parameters in the web-based management, which a root helper then runs (CVSS v3.1 8.8); CVE-2026-88850 lets low-privileged users change root-owned PROFIBUS parameters (v3.1 8.1). Firmware 4.10.0 (FW32) fixes both. ICSA-26-293-01 covers six local flaws in HMS Networks’ PEAK-System PCAN Windows CAN drivers, 5.1.2 and earlier, that can crash the Windows kernel; the highest, CVE-2026-103672, is v3.1 7.1, driver 5.1.4 fixes them, and CISA says they are not remotely exploitable. The batch also covers Moxa’s AIG-302 edge gateway, where a hard-coded cryptographic key (CVE-2026-109813, v3.1 8.1 / v4.0 8.6) is fixed in 1.4.1, plus two Hitachi Energy revisions. None is reported exploited. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: WAGO sells a PFC200 XTR variant it describes as ideal for the railway industry and its controllers are common in building services, while PCAN adapters are a usual way to connect a maintenance laptop to a vehicle’s CAN network.

items.title: CISA republishes Siemens’ October advisories and the S7 PLC web-server flaws (CVSS 9.6) still have no fix — alongside October’s Rockwell ArmorBlock takeover and RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW fixes
items.content_text: CISA republished Siemens’ October advisories on 22 October as ICSA-26-295-02 to -18, including the exploited Software Center flaw covered in its own card above, and several products still have no fix: the S7 PLC web server across 157 listed S7-1500, ET 200SP and related products, where Siemens says it is preparing fixes; the GNU/Linux subsystems of the S7-1500 CPU 1518(F)-4 PN/DP MFP and the TM MFP module; WinCC V7.5; and APOGEE MBC/MEC and Desigo PXC/PXM building controllers, for which no fix is planned. CISA lists Transportation Systems among the sectors. Siemens published the originals on 13 October, 17 new advisories by SecurityWeek’s count. The most serious, SSA-591731, covers eight web-server flaws in SIMATIC S7-1500, ET 200SP and ET 200pro CPUs and drive controllers, rated CVSS v3.1 9.6 by Siemens: an attacker can run code in an authorised user’s browser and perform PLC operations with that user’s rights. All versions are affected and only mitigations are available so far. SSA-832641 fixes authenticated path-traversal flaws in Industrial Edge devices (up to CVSS v3.1 9.1), with no fix yet for SCALANCE LPE9413 and LPE9433 or the affected HMI panels; SSA-784472 lists 377 CVEs in the optional Linux subsystem of the S7-1500 TM MFP technology module, also unfixed. SSA-508506 covers 11 flaws in RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW, including SQL injection and retrieval of administrator credentials, up to CVSS 8.8, fixed in V6.0. Rockwell’s only new advisory, SD1801, covers 1732E ArmorBlock I/O modules at 3.012 and earlier: CVE-2026-12655 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) lets an unauthenticated attacker change the web-server password and take over the module, and CVE-2026-12656 is a network-storm denial of service that needs a power cycle to clear; 3.013 fixes both. Schneider Electric issued SEVD-2026-286-02 for Sage RTUs that do not sufficiently verify firmware authenticity, fixed in C3414-500-S02L0, and SEVD-2026-286-01 for an unmaintained third-party component in Pro-face STW6000 and Harmony STW6 HMIs. None of these is reported exploited or listed in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: S7-1500 and ET 200SP controllers are common in depot, workshop, tunnel-ventilation and station plant; APOGEE and Desigo controllers run building heating and ventilation; CROSSBOW is built to manage remote access to substation devices, a model traction-power estates also use; and RTUs of the Sage type can sit in traction-power and pumping SCADA.

items.title: CISA’s 6–15 October ICS advisories: an end-of-life building controller and a camera platform labelled for transportation, both unfixable, plus N-Tron switches and Ignition
items.content_text: CISA published ICS advisories on 6, 8, 13 and 15 October. Two list Transportation Systems among the sectors using the affected products, and neither has a fix. ICSA-26-279-01 republishes Johnson Controls’ JCI-PSA-2026-12 for EasyIO FG controller firmware: hard-coded credentials (CVE-2026-27872) and improper privilege management (CVE-2026-27873), each CVSS v3.1 7.7. The product is end-of-life, no fix will be issued, and Johnson Controls advises migrating to EasyIO Neo; CISA notes high attack complexity and that the flaws are not remotely exploitable. ICSA-26-288-02 covers Guangzhou Juan IoT’s EseeCloud app and firmware, used in low-cost IP cameras and recorders: hard-coded credentials at CVSS 9.8 (CVE-2026-107617) plus two medium flaws, and the vendor did not respond to CISA. Beyond the transport label, ICSA-26-281-01 covers seven flaws in Red Lion N-Tron 700 Series industrial Ethernet switches reported by Idaho National Laboratory, including factory administrator credentials that stay active, unauthenticated SNMP configuration changes and unsigned firmware updates (highest CVSS v3.1 8.3; the authentication bypass needs physical access); firmware 3.11.1 fixes them, and CISA updated the scores on 15 October. ICSA-26-286-01 covers a privilege-escalation flaw in Inductive Automation’s Ignition SCADA platform (CVE-2026-92817, CVSS v3.1 8.8), fixed in 8.1.55 and 8.3.9, and ICSA-26-288-01 six flaws in the open-source Eclipse Milo OPC UA library, fixed in 1.1.5 with no fix for the 0.6.x line. For energy, ICSA-26-279-06 covers Hitachi Energy’s end-of-life RTU500 CMU firmware, where CVE-2026-8065 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) allows unauthenticated firmware upload; the remedy is moving to supported firmware 12.7.8 or 13.9.1. CISA reports no known exploitation for any of them, and none is in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: EasyIO-class controllers run station heating, ventilation and lighting; low-cost camera platforms turn up at depots and car parks; N-Tron switches carry plant-room networks; Ignition is a common SCADA and HMI layer for station and facility systems; and RTU500 units can sit in traction-power substations.

items.title: Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager and Fortinet FortiMail join KEV as exploited zero-days — one configures the routers at every station and depot, the other screens mail into the corporate side
items.content_text: Cisco published an advisory on 30 September for CVE-2026-76504 in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager: improper handling of URI encoding lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker get past an authentication rule meant to protect an API endpoint and reach administrative-level access. Cisco scores it CVSS 9.8, offers no workaround, and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September; CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 3 October deadline, and Cisco revised the advisory on 2 October. Fixed releases are 20.9.10.1, 20.12.8.2, 20.15.6.1, 20.18.4.1, 26.1.2.1 and 26.2.1, and releases older than 20.9 must migrate to a fixed one. On 1 October Fortinet disclosed CVE-2026-104286 in FortiMail (FG-IR-26-175), a path-traversal and NULL-byte handling flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the appliance through crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Fortinet scores it CVSS 9.8 and says it has been reported exploited in the wild; CISA added it to KEV on 1 October with a 4 October deadline. Affected are FortiMail 7.2.0 to 7.2.9, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6 and 8.0.0 to 8.0.1; Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2, and tells 7.2 customers to move to 7.4 or later. Neither vendor has named an actor or victims, and nothing ties either flaw to rail. The rail fit is our editorial assessment: SD-WAN Manager is the controller that pushes configuration and policy to the edge routers in stations, depots, yards and wayside communication huts, so administrative access there is a route to rewriting segmentation at every site at once; FortiMail sits on the corporate side, where a compromised mail gateway can read, alter or send the messages that open most intrusions against dispatch and operations staff.

items.title: MikroTik: the exploited “MikroTrick” SSH chain is in KEV with every deadline passed, and CISA adds a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication web-management flaw that is not — the router class that quietly backhauls remote rail sites
items.content_text: CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue holds three MikroTik RouterOS flaws: CVE-2026-86060, an argument-injection flaw, and CVE-2026-67277, a missing-authentication flaw in the bandwidth-test service, both added on 10 September; and CVE-2026-67279, an SSH flaw added on 25 September that lets an unauthenticated client open a session channel and send an exec request and, in KEV’s words, “can be chained to achieve unauthenticated exploitation of CVE-2026-86060”. The federal deadlines of 13 and 28 September have both passed. CERT Polska reported on 5 September that this SSH chain, which it calls MikroTrick, had been exploited in the wild since about 2 September, before patches existed, and its 22 September analysis confirms that CVE-2026-67279 combined with CVE-2026-86060 gives an unauthenticated attacker full administrative control. CVE-2026-67276, which some earlier coverage placed in the chain, is not in KEV. Fixed builds for the chain are RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21, plus 7.25beta3; a related flaw, CVE-2026-67278, needs 7.24.3 or 7.23.6 because the earlier fix was incomplete. On 29 September CISA published advisory ICSA-26-272-06 for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-84411: an integer underflow in RouterOS’s HTTP request-body handling, reachable before authentication, that can give remote code execution as root, or a denial of service, from a single crafted request. It is scored CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 9.3, affects versions before 7.24 and is fixed from 7.24; CISA reports no known public exploitation, and it is not in KEV. Read literally, CISA’s affected range takes in the 7.23 and 6.49 builds that fix the SSH chain, so check MikroTik’s release notes before treating a device on those lines as covered. No victims, sectors or actor have been named for any of these flaws, and nothing ties the activity to rail. The relevance for this audience is our editorial assessment: low-cost RouterOS hardware, including its cellular models, is a common choice for backhaul and telemetry at remote, unstaffed sites such as crossings, wayside cabinets, yard offices and small stations, and a router compromised at that layer sits upstream of whatever segmentation you rely on.

items.title: CISA’s 29 September and 1 October ICS batches lean on transport: a Lantronix cellular gateway whose firmware checks can be defeated, IP cameras at CVSS 10.0 with public exploit code, and an EV-charging platform with no version fix
items.content_text: CISA published seven ICS advisories on 29 September (ICSA-26-272-01 to -07) and six on 1 October (ICSA-26-274-01 to -06), and more than half of them list Transportation Systems among the sectors using the affected products. The one closest to rail infrastructure is ICSA-26-272-01, for the Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateway: firmware 2.6.0.4R6_stable carries an improper verification of cryptographic signature flaw (CVE-2026-91191) and a cross-site scripting flaw (CVE-2026-84409), each CVSS v3.1 7.5 and v4 7.7, which CISA says could allow an attacker to replace software and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. Version 2.6.0.7R6 fixes both, and CISA names Transportation Systems, Energy, and Water and Wastewater as the sectors. ICSA-26-272-03 covers command injection in VIVOTEK camera firmware across 37 models (CVE-2026-22755, CVSS v3.1 10.0 and v4 9.3), for which public proof-of-concept code exists; the fix is current firmware. ICSA-26-274-02 covers every version of Monta’s monta.app EV-charging platform, where missing authentication on a WebSocket interface allows charging-station impersonation (CVE-2026-95102, CVSS v3.1 9.4 and v4 9.3); there is no fixed version, only Monta’s guidance to enable OCPP 1.6 Security Profile 2 and its statement that rate limiting is in place. ICSA-26-274-01 covers Armatura One physical access control below 4.7.2 (USA builds below 4.6.1), which embeds an ActiveMQ component carrying CVE-2023-46604 — a flaw already in KEV from attacks on other ActiveMQ deployments, though none is reported against Armatura — plus hard-coded keys and credentials; 4.7.2 and 4.6.1_USA fix it. The other transport-labelled items are the Viidure dashcam Android app, with hard-coded cloud credentials (CVSS 10.0) and no fix planned; two lower-scored, fixed Johnson Controls EasyIO Neo controller flaws; and Toptech TMS7 and TopHAT terminal-management software, with a CVSS 10.0 flaw fixed in 7.8. CISA reports no known exploitation for any advisory in either batch. The MikroTik advisory in the 29 September batch is covered in its own card. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: cellular gateways of the G520 type backhaul crossings, wayside cabinets, substations and vehicle telemetry; IP cameras and access control sit in every station; and transit agencies electrifying bus fleets run depot charging platforms of exactly the Monta type.

items.title: Two critical lwIP flaws in two weeks — the MQTT client on 22 September, the SMTP client on 6 October — and the question is still which field devices ship them
items.content_text: CISA has now published two critical advisories for lwIP, the lightweight open-source TCP/IP stack built into a very wide range of embedded controllers, gateways, I/O modules and sensors. On 6 October ICSA-26-279-02 covered a classic buffer overflow in the SMTP client application of lwIP 2.2.1 (CVE-2026-15340, CVSS v3.1 9.8 per the advisory and v4.0 9.3 per the CVE record); the fix is an upstream patch and commit rather than a new release, and CISA names energy and water as the sectors. It follows ICSA-26-265-01 on 22 September, an out-of-bounds write in lwIP’s MQTT client (CVE-2026-87121, CVSS 9.8 v3.1 and 9.3 v4.0, network-reachable with no authentication or user interaction) that may give an attacker full code execution on the device; it was reported by Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay. A separate double-free advisory published the same day, ICSA-26-265-02, was reported by Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security; we could not verify its CVE or score, so none is quoted. Because lwIP is a library, exposure depends on whether a device maker compiled in the affected client application, and no downstream vendor list has been published for either flaw. The 22 September batch also carried two Siemens advisories that touch station estates: an unrestricted file upload in Siveillance Control, Siemens’ physical-security management platform, and a code-injection flaw in the Desigo CC building-management family, reported by Michelin CERT. No exploitation is reported for any of these. For rail, the plausible lwIP carriers are the telemetry gateways, condition-monitoring sensors and small controllers in traction-power, tunnel-ventilation and wayside cabinets, many of which publish over MQTT or send alarm email.

items.title: Rockwell extends its lockout-recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850, and MITRE now catalogues the PLC-tampering campaign behind it as C0066
items.content_text: Rockwell Automation published revision 5.0 of security notice SD1790 on 18 September, its fifth revision since the notice first appeared on 30 July. The notice exists because of an FBI public service announcement of 30 July describing attackers who remotely altered the configuration of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers, changed IP addresses and set passwords where none had existed, locking the operators out. The original guidance covered MicroLogix 1100 and 1400; revision 5.0 extends the hardening and password-recovery instructions to the Micro820 and Micro850 controllers as well. There is no CVE: the notice is about exposure and configuration, not a software flaw. The controls Rockwell lists are the familiar ones — remove the controller from any internet-reachable path, put access behind a VPN and firewall, set strong passwords, keep offline backups of the project so a locked controller can be restored, disable the built-in HTTP server and keep firmware current. The revision adds no new incident data. MITRE has since documented the July 2026 intrusions behind that PSA as campaign C0066 in ATT&CK v20 (page created 8 October, updated 13 October): more than 30 Minnesota municipal water and wastewater utilities whose internet-facing MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers had IP addresses and passwords changed, with program logic altered at one or more victims; MITRE says the campaign has not been formally attributed. Our assessment of the rail relevance: MicroLogix and Micro800-class controllers are the low-cost PLCs that end up in small, distributed installations built by contractors — pump and drainage stations, tunnel and station plant, yard equipment, small traction-power auxiliaries — often with a cellular modem for remote support and no entry in the operator’s OT asset register. The FBI describes a class of attack that needs no exploit at all, just reachability.

items.title: CISA’s four-year strategy, “CISA 2030”, puts operational technology and consequence-based prioritisation at its centre — with a review of core services due to start within 60 days
items.content_text: CISA released its strategic plan, CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, on 26 October. Acting Director Nick Andersen describes a shift from passive defence to an anticipatory stance, and the plan says the agency will move away from threat-agnostic, all-hazards approaches toward risk-informed, consequence-based analysis. It names OT security — asset visibility and intrusion detection — among its priorities, alongside third-party and supply-chain guidance and support for a national risk register. CISA will begin a review of its core services within 60 days, deliver an implementation plan with metrics within 180 days and report progress after a year. The plan creates no new legal authorities and no new obligations for operators. Analysts quoted by GovInfoSecurity question how quickly the agency can deliver it with reduced staffing. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: a consequence-based CISA is likely to start conversations by asking which systems would hurt most if lost, and operators who have already ranked their own — dispatch, signalling support, traction power, passenger information — will be better placed in those conversations and in their TSA assessments.

items.title: The OT Cybersecurity Coalition asks CISA for a binding directive on federal agencies’ own OT — a proposal, landing days after GAO found only 7 of 22 civilian agencies fully meet the device rules already in place
items.content_text: The OT Cybersecurity Coalition, an industry group, published a paper on 6 October, reported by CyberScoop, urging CISA to issue a binding operational directive dedicated to operational technology at federal civilian agencies. It asks that the directive make each agency assign an accountable OT cybersecurity officer, set minimum practices drawn from existing federal guidance, align with CISA’s 2022 Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, and consider whether past NSA OT guidance should apply to civilian agencies. In the coalition’s words, “it is time for an encompassing BOD solely focused on OT security.” Earlier directives (BOD 23-01, 23-02 and 26-04) touched OT without being dedicated to it. The coalition cites GAO-26-108937, published on 30 September, which reviewed 22 civilian CFO Act agencies against OMB requirements for networked IoT and OT devices: 15 had established inventories, 11 maintained them, 10 included all required information, and only 7 fully met all three. GAO notes that OMB has yet to issue updated guidance covering fiscal year 2026 and recommends that it do so. CISA did not respond to CyberScoop and has announced no such directive. On 14 October, after the French supermarket refrigeration attack, the coalition said failures in cybersecurity fundamentals had led to a significant incident, repeated the French cyber agency’s advice on VPN-only access, default passwords and firmware, and renewed its call for the directive, while noting that no US incidents of that kind have been reported. A directive of this kind would bind federal civilian agencies only — not railroads, transit authorities or their contractors. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: federal directives tend to become the reference for what regulators and auditors later expect of operators, and the requirements the coalition lists — a named OT owner, an inventory that is maintained rather than compiled once, minimum practices tied to the performance goals — are the ones TSA assessments already probe.

items.title: CISA’s “Securing the Next 250” campaign boils critical-infrastructure advice down to reduce, replace, recover — and “replace” means the end-of-support kit railways keep longest
items.content_text: CISA has launched Securing the Next 250 for Cybersecurity Awareness Month, a voluntary campaign aimed at critical-infrastructure owners and operators, state and local governments and individuals, reported by Industrial Cyber on 2 October. Its organising idea is three Rs: reduce attack surfaces, replace end-of-support devices, and recover quickly to sustain operations. For individuals it repeats four practices: avoid and report phishing, use strong and unique passwords, turn on multifactor authentication and password managers, and keep software updated. Acting Director Nick Andersen framed the campaign around the knock-on effect a disruption has on the businesses and communities that depend on vital services. The campaign creates no new obligation and does not single out transportation. It is here because the three Rs map unusually well onto rail estates, where equipment lifecycles run to decades: reduce is the internet-facing remote-access and edge gear driving this page’s threat level, replace is the unsupported operating systems and network devices left in signalling support, passenger information and station plant, and recover is the manual-working plan that keeps trains moving when those systems are lost. That reading is our editorial assessment.

items.title: GAO’s industry panel says overlapping cyber-reporting rules pull responders away from containment — and CIRCIA’s final rule, logged for White House review on 1 October, remains pending
items.content_text: GAO published GAO-26-109197 on 28 September, Cybersecurity Regulations: Industry Panelists Identify Duplication and Conflicts and Ways to Address Them. It records a virtual panel held on 16 July 2026 with six industry representatives from energy, financial services, and healthcare and public health, who said it could be difficult to satisfy every reporting requirement while also remediating a threat, and who saw DHS and SEC rules as duplicating sector-specific ones. Half of the participants agreed that progress on harmonisation has been limited. Their suggestions were consistent timeframes, thresholds and definitions; a lead agency such as CISA to coordinate reporting; and closer government–industry collaboration. The report makes no formal GAO recommendations, and no rail or transit participant is listed. It follows analysis published on 8 September by the McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, citing earlier GAO work, that counted 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which reach private industry. The rule that would add another federal clock, CISA’s CIRCIA final rule, carried a September 2026 target in the federal regulatory agenda; the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs logged it for review on 1 October, and we found no published final text as of 28 October, so its 72-hour incident and 24-hour ransom-payment reporting duties are not yet in force and could still change. Rail sits in an unusually crowded corner of this map: a single event at a transit authority can trigger the 72-hour report to CISA required under the TSA security directives, an FTA or state safety oversight notification, a local emergency-management report and a breach notification if rider or payment data is involved — and, once it is final, CIRCIA as well.
